title: Swords into ploughshares (Isaiah 2:4)
hookLine: nations shall not learn war any more

lines: A BRONZE MAN WITH A HAMMER.
A GIFT IN THE COLD WAR.
cards: In the garden of the United Nations in New York there's a bronze statue of a muscular man swinging a hammer. In one hand he holds a sword, and he's bending its blade into the curved shape of a plough.
It was a gift from the Soviet Union in 1959, at the height of the Cold War, which is its own kind of irony. The idea it shows is about twenty-seven centuries old.
It comes from the prophet Isaiah, from a vision so stubborn and so hopeful that both superpowers could stand in front of it and want it.

teach.b: Isaiah sees a day when the mountain of the Lord's house is lifted above every hill, and the nations stream to it. Not marched there. Streaming, the way rivers flow, except uphill.
And they say to each other: come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and he will teach us his ways.
Then the line, in the Douay-Rheims: "they shall turn their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles: nation shall not lift up sword against nation."
The verse ends: "neither shall they be exercised any more to war." It's better known as: they shall not learn war any more. A sword is iron.
So is the blade of a plough.
Same metal, reshaped. Isaiah doesn't imagine weapons vanishing. He imagines them hammered, by hand, into tools that feed people.
The energy that went into killing goes into harvest. And notice the order. First the nations come to learn God's ways.

teach.h: FIRST LEARN, THEN BEAT THE SWORDS.
teach.b: Then they beat their swords. Peace in this vision isn't just a ceasefire. It comes from learning a different way to live.
The same words appear almost exactly in the prophet Micah.
And the prophet Joel turns them inside out in a call to battle: beat your ploughshares into swords.

teach.h: NATION SHALL NOT LIFT UP SWORD AGAINST NATION.
teach.b: The Bible knows both directions are possible.

The Catholic Church opens Advent with this reading in one year of the cycle, and Pope John the Twenty-Third's letter Pacem in Terris, Peace on Earth, written in 1963, carried the same hope into the nuclear age.

how: Catholics hear Isaiah's vision of peace on the First Sunday of Advent in one year of the Lectionary, and the Church's teaching on peace, from Pacem in Terris onward, returns to it often.

o: a sword, the weapon beaten into a farm tool
a spear, the weapon turned into a sickle
a plow blade used to break up the soil

games.q: the vision of peace — tap the pairs.
p: stream up to the mountain of the Lord

s: in Isaiah's vision the weapons simply disappear
they're hammered into farm tools. the same iron is reshaped.
almost the same words appear in the prophet Micah
Micah 4:3 repeats the swords and ploughshares line.
the Bible only ever uses this image for peace
Joel reverses it in a call to war: beat your ploughshares into swords.

games.q: you're one of the nations in Isaiah's vision. you've come up the mountain and been taught God's ways. what happens next?
o: you sign a treaty and keep your swords.
you beat your swords into ploughshares.
you go home and teach others to fight better.
games.why: after learning God's ways and having their disputes settled, they reshape their weapons into tools, and learn war no more.

practice: Name one small war in your life, a cold standoff with a sibling, a running argument at work, a grudge you've sharpened for years, and the sword you keep ready for it: a remark, a silence used as a weapon.
Picture hammering it, slowly, into something useful, a question instead of an accusation, a first step instead of waiting for theirs. If you pray, ask for help to put it down.

wordCard.voice: cherev. Hebrew for sword, the weapon Isaiah pictures nations reshaping into farm tools, because they have learned God's ways and will not learn war any more. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: sword. In Isaiah's vision the cherev is beaten into a tool for the field.

carryVoice: Your line: ploughshares. Same iron, made into something that feeds. That's day four hundred seventeen.
